q: A reversible reaction in a closed vessel is at chemical equilibrium when:
o: The concentrations of reactants and products become equal
The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
Both the forward and the reverse reactions stop
All the reactants have been converted into products
x: Equilibrium is reached when the forward and reverse rates become equal. Concentrations then stay constant, but they are usually not equal to each other.

q: Which statement about the concentrations in a mixture at chemical equilibrium is correct?
o: They are always equal for reactants and products
They keep rising for products and falling for reactants
They remain constant with time but are usually not equal to each other
They change continuously in a regular cycle
x: At equilibrium the amounts no longer change because both reactions run at the same rate. Constant does not mean equal: the ratio is fixed by Kc.

q: A state of chemical equilibrium can be set up only when a reversible reaction is carried out:
o: In an open beaker, so that gases can leave
Only in the presence of a catalyst
Only at a very high temperature
In a closed system, so that no substance escapes
x: Products must stay in contact with each other to react back, so a closed system is needed. A catalyst only speeds up the approach to equilibrium; it is not required for it.

q: Which of the following reactions is treated as irreversible, i.e. it goes practically to completion?
o: H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI in a closed flask
CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (burning of methane)
N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂ in a sealed tube
PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂ in a closed vessel
x: Combustion of methane goes to completion and the products do not re-form methane and oxygen. The other three are standard textbook examples of reversible reactions that reach equilibrium.

q: Chemical equilibrium is described as dynamic because:
o: The forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates
The reaction stops once the products are formed
The concentrations of all substances keep changing
The temperature of the mixture keeps changing
x: At equilibrium the reactions have not stopped; molecules keep reacting in both directions at the same rate, so there is no net change in composition.

q: Pure HI is heated to 450 °C in a closed flask. Which statement is correct?
o: No reaction occurs, because equilibrium can only be reached from the reactant side
The HI decomposes completely into H₂ and I₂
A different value of Kc is obtained because the reaction started from the product side
H₂ and I₂ form until equilibrium is reached, with the same Kc as when starting from H₂ and I₂
x: Equilibrium can be approached from either direction. At the same temperature the same Kc is reached whether one starts from H₂ and I₂ or from HI.

q: H₂ and I₂ are mixed in a closed flask at a fixed temperature. How do the rates of the forward and reverse reactions change until equilibrium is reached?
o: The forward rate rises and the reverse rate falls until they become equal
The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they become equal
Both rates rise steadily until the reaction stops
Both rates fall to zero at equilibrium
x: At the start only reactants are present, so the forward rate is highest and the reverse rate is zero. As HI builds up the forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until the two are equal.

q: A little radioactive iodine is added to an equilibrium mixture of H₂, I₂ and HI. After some time, radioactivity is found in the HI molecules too. This shows that:
o: The equilibrium has shifted completely towards HI
Radioactive iodine acts as a catalyst
The forward and reverse reactions are still going on at equilibrium
The value of Kc has increased
x: Labelled iodine can only get into HI if I₂ is still reacting with H₂ and HI is still breaking down. This is evidence that equilibrium is dynamic, even though the overall composition does not change.

q: A reversible reaction in a closed vessel never goes to completion because:
o: The products react with each other to re-form the reactants
The reactants are used up too slowly
The catalyst is used up during the reaction
The temperature of the vessel falls as the reaction proceeds
x: As soon as products form, the reverse reaction starts. When its rate equals the forward rate, there is no further net change, so some reactants always remain.

q: A reaction that can proceed in both the forward and the backward directions under the same conditions is called:
o: An irreversible reaction
A reversible reaction
A chain reaction
A displacement reaction
x: A reversible reaction can go both ways under the same conditions; it is shown with the ⇌ sign. An irreversible reaction goes in one direction only.

q: The Kc expression for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is:
o: [N₂][H₂]³ / [NH₃]²
[NH₃] / [N₂][H₂]
[NH₃]² / [N₂][H₂]³
2[NH₃] / [N₂] 3[H₂]
x: Kc is products over reactants, each concentration raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation. Coefficients become powers, not multipliers.

q: For the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), the equilibrium constant Kc is:
o: [SO₂]²[O₂] / [SO₃]²
[SO₃] / [SO₂][O₂]
[SO₃]² / [SO₂]²[O₂]
[SO₃]² / [SO₂][O₂]²
x: SO₃ is the product with coefficient 2; SO₂ has coefficient 2 and O₂ has 1. So Kc = [SO₃]² / [SO₂]²[O₂]. The inverted expression would be Kc for the reverse reaction.

q: For which equilibrium does Kc have no units?
o: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
x: Kc has no units when the total moles in the expression are the same on both sides. For H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI there are 2 on each side, so the units cancel.

q: What are the units of Kc for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)?
o: mol² dm⁻⁶
mol dm⁻³
No units
mol⁻² dm⁶
x: Kc = [NH₃]²/[N₂][H₂]³ has units (mol dm⁻³)² / (mol dm⁻³)⁴ = (mol dm⁻³)⁻², which is mol⁻² dm⁶.

q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), the equilibrium concentrations are [H₂] = 0.1, [I₂] = 0.1 and [HI] = 0.8 mol dm⁻³. What is Kc?
x: Kc = [HI]² / [H₂][I₂] = 0.64 / 0.01 = 64. Forgetting to square [HI] gives 80, and inverting the expression gives about 0.0156.

q: At a certain temperature Kc for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI is 50. At the same temperature, Kc for 2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂ is:
x: Reversing a reaction inverts its equilibrium constant: Kc = 1/50 = 0.02. An equilibrium constant can never be negative.

q: A reaction has a very large value of Kc, such as 10³⁰, at 25 °C. This means that at equilibrium:
o: The mixture is mainly reactants
The mixture is mainly products, so the reaction goes almost to completion
The reaction reaches equilibrium very quickly
Reactants and products are present in equal amounts
x: Kc has products on top, so a very large Kc means the equilibrium lies far to the right. Kc says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached.

q: 1.0 mol of PCl₅ is heated in a 1 dm³ closed vessel: PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂. At equilibrium 0.5 mol of PCl₅ is left. What is Kc?
o: 2.0 mol dm⁻³
0.25 mol dm⁻³
0.5 mol dm⁻³
1.0 mol dm⁻³
x: 0.5 mol PCl₅ reacted, giving 0.5 mol each of PCl₃ and Cl₂. Kc = (0.5 × 0.5)/0.5 = 0.5 mol dm⁻³. Inverting gives 2.0.

q: The numerical value of Kc for a given reaction changes only when:
o: More reactant is added
The pressure is increased
A catalyst is added
The temperature is changed
x: Kc is constant at a given temperature. Changing concentration or pressure shifts the position of equilibrium, but the system re-adjusts to the same Kc; a catalyst changes neither.

q: For a reaction Kc = 4 at a certain temperature. A mixture at this temperature has a reaction quotient Qc = 1. What will happen?
o: Net forward reaction takes place until Qc becomes 4
Net reverse reaction takes place until Qc becomes 4
Nothing, because the mixture is already at equilibrium
Kc falls to 1 to match the mixture
x: When Qc is less than Kc there are too few products, so the forward reaction goes on until Qc = Kc. Kc itself does not change at constant temperature.

q: Le Chatelier's principle states that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in conditions, the system:
o: Shifts its equilibrium position so as to partly undo the change
Stops reacting until the change is removed
Always shifts towards the products
Changes its Kc to match the new conditions
x: The equilibrium moves in the direction that opposes the applied change, such as using up added reactant or absorbing added heat. It does not always favour products.

q: More N₂ is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at constant temperature and volume. What happens?
o: The equilibrium shifts to the right and more NH₃ forms
The equilibrium shifts to the left and NH₃ decomposes
The equilibrium does not change
The value of Kc increases
x: Adding a reactant is opposed by using it up, so the forward reaction is favoured and more NH₃ forms. Kc is unchanged because the temperature is constant.

q: In the reversible reaction CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, the water formed is removed continuously. The effect is that:
o: More ester is formed, because the equilibrium shifts to the right
Less ester is formed, because the equilibrium shifts to the left
The reaction stops
The equilibrium constant becomes zero
x: Removing a product is opposed by forming more of it, so the forward reaction is favoured and the yield of ester rises.

q: The pressure on the equilibrium N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) is increased at constant temperature. The equilibrium shifts:
o: To the right, because more gas molecules are on that side
To the left, because fewer gas molecules are on that side
To the right, because Kc increases with pressure
Neither way, because pressure never affects equilibrium
x: Higher pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas. There is 1 mol on the left and 2 mol on the right, so the equilibrium moves to the left.

q: A change in pressure has no effect on the position of which equilibrium?
o: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)
H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
x: Pressure only matters when the number of gas moles differs on the two sides. H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI has 2 mol of gas on each side.

q: The forward reaction of an equilibrium is exothermic. If the temperature is raised:
o: The equilibrium shifts to the right and Kc increases
The equilibrium shifts to the left but Kc stays the same
The equilibrium shifts to the left and Kc decreases
The position and Kc stay the same
x: Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, which here is the reverse reaction. Fewer products at equilibrium means Kc becomes smaller.

q: N₂O₄ (colourless) ⇌ 2NO₂ (brown). A sealed tube of the equilibrium mixture becomes darker brown when heated. This shows that:
o: The forward reaction is endothermic
The forward reaction is exothermic
Heating has acted as a catalyst
Heating has decreased the value of Kc
x: Darker colour means more NO₂, so heating shifted the equilibrium to the right. Heat favours the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction is endothermic and Kc rises.

q: A catalyst is added to a reaction mixture before it reaches equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
o: Equilibrium is reached sooner, but its composition is the same
More product is present at equilibrium
Less product is present at equilibrium
The value of Kc increases
x: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally. Equilibrium is reached faster, but the equilibrium composition and Kc do not change.

q: For 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH is negative. Which single change increases the equilibrium yield of SO₃?
o: Increasing the temperature
Adding a catalyst
Increasing the pressure
Removing some O₂
x: 3 mol of gas give 2 mol, so higher pressure shifts the equilibrium right. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, a catalyst does not change the yield, and removing O₂ shifts it left.

q: For an equilibrium whose forward reaction is endothermic, raising the temperature:
o: Shifts the equilibrium to the left and decreases Kc
Shifts the equilibrium to the right but leaves Kc unchanged
Shifts the equilibrium to the right and increases Kc
Has no effect, because only pressure affects equilibrium
x: Added heat is absorbed by the endothermic direction, so more products form. Since Kc depends on temperature, it increases.

q: 2CrO₄²⁻ (yellow) + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ (orange) + H₂O. When dilute acid is added to a yellow chromate solution, it turns orange because:
o: Added H⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the left
Added H⁺ shifts the equilibrium to the right
The acid acts as a catalyst
The acid lowers the value of Kc
x: H⁺ is a reactant, so adding it shifts the equilibrium to the right, forming more orange dichromate. Adding alkali removes H⁺ and turns the solution yellow again.

q: The solubility product (Ksp) of a sparingly soluble salt is:
o: The mass of salt that dissolves in 100 g of water
The concentration of the undissolved solid
The sum of the concentrations of its ions in any solution
The product of the molar concentrations of its ions in a saturated solution, each raised to the power of its coefficient
x: Ksp is the equilibrium constant for a saturated solution: the product of the ion concentrations, each raised to its coefficient. The solid does not appear in the expression.

q: The Ksp expression for calcium fluoride, CaF₂, is:
o: [Ca²⁺][F⁻]²
[Ca²⁺][F⁻]
[Ca²⁺]²[F⁻]
x: CaF₂ ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻. The coefficient 2 becomes a power, so Ksp = [Ca²⁺][F⁻]².

q: Silver chromate dissolves as Ag₂CrO₄ ⇌ 2Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻. Its Ksp is:
o: [Ag⁺][CrO₄²⁻]²
[Ag⁺][CrO₄²⁻]
[Ag₂CrO₄] / [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻]
[Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻]
x: Two Ag⁺ ions and one CrO₄²⁻ ion form, so Ksp = [Ag⁺]²[CrO₄²⁻]. The solid salt is not included in the expression.

q: The Ksp expression for calcium phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂, is:
o: [Ca²⁺]²[PO₄³⁻]³
[Ca²⁺][PO₄³⁻]
[3Ca²⁺][2PO₄³⁻]
[Ca²⁺]³[PO₄³⁻]²
x: Ca₃(PO₄)₂ ⇌ 3Ca²⁺ + 2PO₄³⁻, so Ksp = [Ca²⁺]³[PO₄³⁻]². Swapping the powers is a common mistake.

q: The solubility of AgCl in water at 25 °C is 1 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. What is its Ksp?
x: AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, so [Ag⁺] = [Cl⁻] = s. Ksp = s² = (1 × 10⁻⁵)² = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰. 4 × 10⁻¹⁰ would come from wrongly using 4s² as for a 1 : 2 salt.

q: The solubility of CaF₂ in water is 2 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³. What is its Ksp?
x: [Ca²⁺] = s and [F⁻] = 2s, so Ksp = s(2s)² = 4s³ = 4 × 8 × 10⁻¹² = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹. Forgetting the 2 gives 8 × 10⁻¹²; forgetting to square gives 8 × 10⁻⁸.

q: A sparingly soluble salt MX (giving M⁺ and X⁻) has Ksp = 9 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is its solubility in pure water?
o: 3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³
9 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³
4.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³
3 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³
x: For MX, Ksp = s², so s = √(9 × 10⁻¹⁰) = 3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Halving Ksp or taking the square root of only the 9 are typical errors.

q: A precipitate of a sparingly soluble salt forms from a solution when:
o: The ionic product is less than its Ksp
The ionic product is exactly zero
The Ksp of the salt becomes zero
The ionic product of its ions exceeds its Ksp
x: If the ionic product is greater than Ksp the solution is supersaturated, so solid separates until the product falls to Ksp. Below Ksp more solid can dissolve.

q: Two solutions are mixed so that [Ag⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁴ and [Cl⁻] = 1 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ in the mixture. Ksp of AgCl = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. What happens?
o: AgCl precipitates, because the ionic product 1 × 10⁻⁸ exceeds Ksp
No precipitate forms, because the ionic product is below Ksp
No precipitate forms, because the ionic product exactly equals Ksp
AgCl precipitates, because the ionic product 2 × 10⁻⁴ exceeds Ksp
x: Ionic product = (1 × 10⁻⁴)(1 × 10⁻⁴) = 1 × 10⁻⁸, which is greater than 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, so AgCl precipitates. Ions are multiplied, not added.

q: Four silver salts of the same formula type have these Ksp values at 25 °C: AgCl 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰, AgBr 5.0 × 10⁻¹³, AgI 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁷, AgSCN 1.0 × 10⁻¹². Which is the least soluble?
o: AgI
AgCl
AgBr
AgSCN
x: For salts of the same formula type, the smallest Ksp means the lowest solubility. 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁷ is the smallest value, so AgI is least soluble.

q: The Ksp of a given sparingly soluble salt changes when:
o: The temperature changes
More solid salt is added
The solution is stirred
A salt with a common ion is added
x: Ksp is an equilibrium constant, so it depends only on temperature. Adding a common ion lowers the solubility, but Ksp stays the same.

q: The common ion effect is:
o: The increase in solubility of a salt when another salt is added
The neutralisation of an acid by a base
The suppression of the ionisation or solubility of an electrolyte by adding another electrolyte with an ion in common
The resistance of a buffer to a change in pH
x: Adding an ion that is already present shifts the equilibrium back, reducing ionisation of a weak electrolyte or the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt.

q: When HCl gas is passed through a saturated solution of sodium chloride, crystals of pure NaCl separate out. This is because:
o: HCl reacts with NaCl to form an insoluble compound
HCl lowers the temperature of the solution
Extra Cl⁻ ions raise the ionic product of NaCl above its solubility product
Na⁺ ions are oxidised by HCl
x: HCl supplies the common ion Cl⁻. The product [Na⁺][Cl⁻] then exceeds the solubility product, so NaCl crystallises. This is used to purify common salt.

q: Adding solid NH₄Cl to a solution of NH₄OH:
o: Increases the ionisation of NH₄OH and raises [OH⁻]
Suppresses the ionisation of NH₄OH and lowers [OH⁻]
Has no effect on the ionisation of NH₄OH
Converts NH₄OH into a strong base
x: NH₄Cl provides the common ion NH₄⁺, which shifts NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ to the left. [OH⁻] falls.

q: Sodium ethanoate (CH₃COONa) is dissolved in a solution of ethanoic acid. The pH of the solution:
o: Falls, because more H⁺ ions are produced
Stays exactly the same
Falls, because sodium ethanoate is a strong acid
Rises, because the ionisation of the acid is suppressed
x: CH₃COO⁻ is a common ion that shifts CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ to the left. Fewer H⁺ ions means a higher pH.

q: Compared with its solubility in pure water, the solubility of AgCl in a dilute NaCl solution is:
o: Higher, because NaCl reacts with AgCl
Lower, because of the common Cl⁻ ion
Exactly the same, because Ksp is constant
Higher, because Na⁺ ions attract Cl⁻ ions
x: Cl⁻ from NaCl is a common ion, so less AgCl needs to dissolve before the ionic product reaches Ksp. Ksp is constant, but the solubility falls.

q: Ksp of AgCl = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is the solubility of AgCl in 0.01 mol dm⁻³ NaCl solution? (Take [Cl⁻] as 0.01 mol dm⁻³.)
o: 1 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³
1 × 10⁻¹² mol dm⁻³
1 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³
1 × 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³
x: s = Ksp / [Cl⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 1 × 10⁻² = 1 × 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³. In pure water it would be 1 × 10⁻⁵; multiplying instead of dividing gives 1 × 10⁻¹².

q: In qualitative analysis, H₂S is passed through an acidified (HCl) solution to precipitate group II sulphides only. The role of HCl is to:
o: Raise [S²⁻] by increasing the ionisation of H₂S
Oxidise H₂S to sulphur
Increase the Ksp of group II sulphides
Lower [S²⁻] by suppressing the ionisation of H₂S
x: H⁺ from HCl is a common ion that suppresses H₂S ⇌ 2H⁺ + S²⁻. The low [S²⁻] exceeds Ksp only for the very insoluble group II sulphides.

q: Which substance, when added to ethanoic acid (acetic acid), suppresses its ionisation by the common ion effect?
o: NaCl
CH₃COONa
KNO₃
Na₂SO₄
x: Only sodium ethanoate supplies CH₃COO⁻, an ion already produced by the acid. NaCl, KNO₃ and Na₂SO₄ share no ion with CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.

q: NH₄Cl is added along with NH₄OH when group III hydroxides (such as Fe(OH)₃ and Al(OH)₃) are precipitated. This is done so that:
o: [OH⁻] becomes very high so that all metal hydroxides precipitate
NH₄OH is converted into a strong base
The Ksp of group III hydroxides is increased
[OH⁻] stays low, and hydroxides of later groups, such as Mg(OH)₂ do not precipitate
x: NH₄⁺ suppresses the ionisation of NH₄OH, so [OH⁻] is just enough to exceed the very small Ksp of group III hydroxides but not that of more soluble hydroxides like Mg(OH)₂.

q: In which of the following, at the same temperature, is the solubility of BaSO₄ the lowest?
o: 0.01 mol dm⁻³ Na₂SO₄ solution
Pure water
0.1 mol dm⁻³ Na₂SO₄ solution
0.1 mol dm⁻³ NaCl solution
x: SO₄²⁻ is a common ion; the higher its concentration, the lower the solubility of BaSO₄ (s = Ksp/[SO₄²⁻]). NaCl shares no ion with BaSO₄.

q: A buffer solution is a solution that:
o: Has a pH of exactly 7
Changes pH sharply when a little acid is added
Resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
Contains only a strong acid and water
x: A buffer keeps its pH almost constant when small amounts of acid or base are added. Buffers can have pH values below or above 7.

q: An acidic buffer can be made by mixing:
o: A weak acid and its salt with a strong base, e.g. CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa
A strong acid and its salt, e.g. HCl and NaCl
A weak base and its salt with a strong acid, e.g. NH₄OH and NH₄Cl
A strong acid and a strong base in equal amounts
x: An acidic buffer contains a weak acid with its conjugate base, e.g. ethanoic acid with sodium ethanoate. NH₄OH with NH₄Cl is a basic buffer.

q: Which pair of substances forms a basic buffer?
o: NaOH and NaCl
NH₄OH and NH₄Cl
CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa
HCl and NH₄Cl
x: A basic buffer is a weak base with its salt of a strong acid: NH₄OH with NH₄Cl. NaOH is a strong base, and ethanoic acid with its salt gives an acidic buffer.

q: Which mixture is NOT a buffer solution?
o: CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa
NH₄OH and NH₄Cl
HCl and NaCl
H₂CO₃ and NaHCO₃
x: HCl is a strong acid; with NaCl there is no weak acid–conjugate base pair to absorb added H⁺ or OH⁻. The other three are each a weak acid or base with its salt.

q: A small amount of HCl is added to a buffer of CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa. The pH hardly changes because the added H⁺ ions:
o: Combine with Na⁺ ions to form NaH
React with CH₃COOH to form more H⁺ ions
Escape from the solution as hydrogen gas
Combine with CH₃COO⁻ ions to form un-ionised CH₃COOH
x: The ethanoate ions act as a reservoir of base: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH. The weak acid formed ionises only slightly, so [H⁺] barely rises.

q: A small amount of NaOH is added to a buffer of CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa. The added OH⁻ ions are removed by:
o: CH₃COO⁻, forming CH₃COOH
Na⁺, forming NaOH
CH₃COOH, forming CH₃COO⁻ and water
Water, forming more OH⁻
x: The weak acid neutralises the base: CH₃COOH + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O. So [OH⁻] barely rises and the pH stays almost constant.

q: The main buffer system that keeps the pH of human blood close to 7.4 is:
o: Hydrochloric acid and sodium chloride
Ammonium hydroxide and ammonium chloride
Carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate (H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻)
Ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate
x: Blood is buffered mainly by H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻, which keeps its pH near 7.4. HCl with NaCl is not a buffer at all.

q: A buffer contains equal concentrations of CH₃COOH and CH₃COONa. The pKa of CH₃COOH is 4.74. What is the pH of the buffer?
x: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]). With equal concentrations the log term is log 1 = 0, so pH = pKa = 4.74. 9.26 is 14 − 4.74.

q: A buffer contains CH₃COONa at 10 times the concentration of CH₃COOH. pKa of CH₃COOH = 4.74. What is the pH?
x: pH = pKa + log([salt]/[acid]) = 4.74 + log 10 = 4.74 + 1 = 5.74. Putting the ratio upside down gives 3.74.

q: A buffer made from NH₄OH and NH₄Cl in equal concentrations has a pH of about:
x: NH₄OH/NH₄Cl is a basic buffer, so its pH is above 7. With equal concentrations pOH = pKb (about 4.75), so pH is about 14 − 4.75 ≈ 9.3.

q: In the Haber process, ammonia is manufactured by the reaction of:
o: Nitrogen and oxygen
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Hydrogen and nitric acid
Nitrogen monoxide and water
x: The Haber process combines nitrogen and hydrogen: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. The forward reaction is exothermic.

q: The catalyst used in the Haber process is:
o: Finely divided iron
Vanadium(V) oxide
Platinum gauze
Finely divided nickel
x: Iron (with promoters) catalyses ammonia synthesis. V₂O₅ is used in the Contact process for SO₃ and nickel in hydrogenation of oils.

q: The temperature used in the Haber process is about:
x: A moderate temperature of roughly 400–500 °C is used. Lower temperatures make the reaction too slow, and much higher ones give a very poor yield.

q: The pressure used in the Haber process is about:
o: 1 atm
5 atm
5000 atm
x: A high pressure of about 200–300 atm is used to favour ammonia. Much higher pressures would need very costly, strong equipment.

q: High pressure increases the yield of ammonia in the Haber process because:
o: 4 moles of gaseous reactants form only 2 moles of gaseous product
The forward reaction is endothermic
High pressure increases the value of Kc
High pressure makes the iron catalyst more active
x: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ goes from 4 mol of gas to 2 mol. By Le Chatelier's principle, high pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules.

q: The formation of ammonia is exothermic, so a low temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield. A low temperature is still NOT used because:
o: The yield of ammonia falls at low temperature
The iron catalyst works only above 1000 °C
Ammonia decomposes at low temperature
The rate becomes too slow, so a compromise temperature is chosen
x: Low temperature favours ammonia at equilibrium but makes the reaction far too slow. About 400–500 °C is an optimum: a reasonable yield obtained at a reasonable rate.

q: What is the purpose of the iron catalyst in the Haber process?
o: It shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia
It increases the value of Kc
It makes equilibrium reach faster but does not increase the equilibrium yield
It absorbs the heat given out by the reaction
x: A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached quickly. It does not change the equilibrium position or Kc.

q: In the Haber process, ammonia is separated from the gas mixture leaving the converter, and the unreacted gases are recycled. Ammonia is separated by:
o: Passing the mixture through concentrated sulphuric acid
Burning off the unreacted hydrogen
Heating the mixture strongly
Cooling, so that ammonia liquefies
x: Ammonia liquefies much more easily than N₂ and H₂, so cooling removes it as a liquid. The unreacted N₂ and H₂ go back to the converter.

q: Very high pressures, far above about 300 atm, would give even more ammonia, but are not used because:
o: Higher pressure would reduce the yield of ammonia
The plant and its compression costs become too expensive and unsafe
Higher pressure would reduce the value of Kc
Higher pressure would stop the iron catalyst working
x: Raising the pressure always favours ammonia here, but very high pressures need very thick, costly vessels and much energy for compression, and are more dangerous.

q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH negative), what happens to Kc when the temperature is raised?
o: It increases
It stays the same
It becomes zero
It decreases
x: The forward reaction is exothermic, so raising the temperature favours the reverse reaction. Less ammonia at equilibrium means a smaller Kc.
